column2: So these two are to be known, the unmanifest and the Person; and what is other and greater than the unmanifest and the Person.
The shrewd should observe that distinction with care: both are without beginning and end, and both are without mark.
Both are eternal, subtler than the subtle, and greater than the great; this is common to both, and the other is a qualification.
By nature, whose law is creation and which has threefold goodness, know the opposite to be the mark of the knower of the field.
The origin marked by union is grasped as born of action; by the instruments of action, whatever the doer does is named by words: "Who am I? This one, that one."
As a man wearing a turban is covered with three cloths, so this embodied one is covered with sattva, rajas and tamas.
Therefore the fourfold is to be known, heaped up by these causes; so that he, being rightly aware, is not bewildered at the time of death.
Wishing for divine fortune, pure in speech and mind regarding Brahman, he should practise stainless austerity with fierce bodily disciplines.
The three worlds are pervaded by austerity, by the shining within; the sun and moon shine in heaven by austerity.
Ardour is the knowledge of austerity, and austerity is so named in the world; the work that dispels rajas and tamas is austerity's own mark.
Celibacy and non-violence are called bodily austerity; restraint of speech and mind and equanimity are called mental austerity.
Food received from twice-born who know the rule is excellent; by restraint in food his rajasic sin is destroyed.
Aversion for objects comes to him and the coverings fall; therefore he should take only as much as is needed here.
At the end of life, by raising the vital force, he should act slowly and not in distress; thus with a joined mind that knowledge is attained.

By rajas too the embodied one moves like one with a body and speech; with mind unobstructed by tasks, standing in nature through detachment, he is freed from the body until its end through heedfulness.
Dissolution of beings, ever with causes, and their creation, do not go beyond what is fixed in the creation of others' belief.

Those whose wisdom is in the end and origin of existence remain in the opposite; bearing bodies by steadiness, with minds cast down by intellect, and being destroyed from their places, they worship them for subtlety.
All that, according to tradition, is not known by intellect; some stay to the end of the body, self-trained and without support; some, joined to concentration, worship being.
They practise the supreme god, the imperishable called lightning; at the time of death, drawing near, their sins burnt by austerity,
all these great souls go to the highest goal; the subtle distinction among them should be observed with the eye of scripture.
Know the supreme body as freed from possession, one of the two beyond the middle air, with a mind attached to concentration.
Those with minds joined to knowledge are freed from the world of mortals; becoming Brahman, stainless, they go then to the highest goal.
Those in whom unwavering knowledge free of passion arises go to the highest worlds, purifying according to strength.
The blessed unborn divine Vishnu, called the unmanifest, they reach by feeling, the pure, satisfied with knowledge, without hope.
Knowing Hari in the self, they do not return; being imperishable, having reached that supreme state, they rejoice in the imperishable undecaying.
This much is the knowledge; this is, and is not; the whole world, bound by craving, revolves like a wheel.
As the fibre of a lotus-stalk lies all through the stalk, so the thread of craving, without beginning or end, always lies in the body.
As the weaver passes the thread through cloth with a needle, so the thread of the world is bound by the needle of craving.
He who rightly knows modification, nature and the eternal Person is satisfied and freed.
This light, the nectar, the blessed sage Narayana spoke out of compassion for beings, for the good of the world."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, by whose conduct the knower of conduct went to great happiness.
Janaka, called Janadeva, lord of men in Mithila, was devoted to reflecting on the dharmas of the state after death.
A hundred teachers ever lived in his house, showing various dharmas, disputants of many heresies.
Regarding the determination of existence after death and birth after death, he stood by tradition and was mostly not satisfied about the truth of the self.
There the great sage Panchashikha, son of Kapila, roaming the whole earth, came also to Mithila.
In the determination of knowledge of truth of all the dharmas of renunciation, with his purpose accomplished, beyond the pairs, his doubts destroyed,
they say he was one of the sages whom desire had settled among men, seeking eternal, utter happiness, so very hard to find.
Him whom the Sankhyas call Kapila, the supreme sage, Prajapati: I think he amazes people in that form himself.
That one-syllabled Brahman which is seen in many forms: Asuri attained that imperishable in that circle.
His pupil Panchashikha was nourished by a human woman's milk; there was a householder brahmana woman named Kapila.
Having become that woman's son, he drank from her breast; thereby he got the name Kapileya and a final understanding.
The blessed one told me this about the birth of Kapileya, his state as Kapileya and his unsurpassed omniscience.
Knowing the commonness, Kapila, the best of the knowers of dharma, approached the hundred teachers and bewildered them with arguments.
Janaka, drawn to him by the sight of the son of Kapila, left the hundred teachers and followed him.
To him, supremely fit and bowed in dharma, he spoke the highest liberation, that which is laid down as Sankhya.
Having spoken of disgust with birth, he spoke of disgust with action; having spoken of disgust with action, he spoke of disgust with all.
That for which one engages in action and for which the fruit of actions arises is unreliable, vain, perishable, unsteady and impermanent.
With destruction seen directly, witnessed by the world, one who says "there is something beyond, from scripture" is defeated.
The non-self is the self's death; affliction, death and old age are fear; he thinks of the self through delusion; that is held to be a poor view.
Now even if it is so, since it is not found in the world, this king thinks he is ageless and deathless.
Is and "is not": in the absence of a mark, what basis could he speak of for deciding the course of the world?
The root of these two, of the end and of tradition, is perception; perceived scripture is not different, nor is the end anything.
Where there is inference here and there, or a thing is made to exist, the soul is held, in the view of the unbelievers, to be other than the body.
Like seed in a hundred drops, like the lodging of cooking ghee, memory of birth, the magnet, the sun-gem, the nature of water,
the passing of beings after death, the praying to deities, and the ceasing of action in the dead: this is held to be authority.
But these are no reasons at all, those that stand in form; for there is no commonness of the immortal with the mortal.
Some say rebirth is from ignorance and the efforts of action; greed and delusion are the cause, and the indulgence of faults.
They call ignorance the field and deed the seed sown; affection engenders craving; this is their rebirth.
When that array is burnt and the thought is of mortal nature, one body is born from another; they call that the end of being.
When he is different in form, birth, scripture and purpose, how can this relation "this is he" be unjoined?
If so, what joy is there in giving, learning, austerity and strength? For all the deed done by one, another gets.
When one here is afflicted by common others, or by the happy or the unhappy, the settlement of it can be seen.
Thus when beaten with clubs, that body would be born again; knowledge, apart from that, by which this is not found, is another.
Season, year, lunar days, cold and heat, dear and undear, as they see them pass, such is the end of being.
When overtaken by old age or by destroying death, the weaker and weaker parts perish first, as in a house.
The senses, mind, breath, blood, flesh and bone perish in order and go to their own constituent.
The arrangement of the world's course, the coming of the fruit of giving and dharma, for which the Vedic words and worldly dealings exist,
so in the mind there are many reasons; "this is, this is" and one reaches nothing at all.
For those so reasoning, running after this and that, the mind settles somewhere and there decays like a tree.
Thus all creatures are pained by gains and losses; they are dragged by traditions as elephants by their drivers.
Many, seeking things that bring utter pleasure, beyond price, fall into greater sorrow, and giving up the bait, go under the power of death.
For the perishable, whose life is unsteady, what use are kinsmen and friends and possessions? He who goes leaving all of it goes in a moment and does not return.
Earth, sky, water, fire and wind ever protect the body; seeing this, where would delight be? There is no ease for this perishable one.
This word, without deceit or trick, the supreme freedom from disease, witnessed by the self, the king, looking at it with astonishment, began to question again.
[Janaka said:] "Blessed one, if there is this name for someone after death, then what will ignorance or knowledge do?
Everything would end in annihilation; see this, best of the twice-born; what difference will careful or careless make?
Non-association with beings, or association with the perishable: for whom is it to be done? What is the truth of the determination here?"
Then to him, as if confused and distressed, covered by darkness, the poet Panchashikha spoke, calming him again with words.
[Panchashikha said:] "There is here no end in annihilation, and no end in being; this aggregate of body, senses and thought goes on separately, yet depending on each other in actions.
These constituents, five-branched: space, wind, fire, water and earth; they stand by nature and are separated by nature.
Space, wind, heat, moisture and the earthy: this fivefold aggregate is called the body in many ways; knowledge, heat and wind are the threefold collection of action.
Senses and their objects, nature, consciousness, mind, prana and apana, modifications and constituents have come out here.
Among them are action and release; the determination of all truths is called the supreme seed, intellect, the great imperishable.
For one who sees this collection of qualities as the self, from wrong views endless sorrow is not stilled.
What is seen as non-self, by that I do not exist and nothing is mine; on what basis then is the series of sorrows attached?
There hear the best treatise on renunciation, called right mind, which will be shown for your liberation.
Renunciation alone of all the actions named, constantly futile and trained, affliction is held to bring sorrow.
In giving up wealth, actions; in giving up enjoyment, vows; in giving up pleasure, the discipline of austerity; in giving up all, completion.
This undivided path of the renunciation of all has been shown, for the abandonment of sorrow; otherwise it would be a bad end.
Having spoken of the five senses of knowledge residing in thought and mind, I shall now tell of the five senses of action residing in the mind.
The hands are the sense of action; the feet the sense of movement; the organ of generation for procreation and delight; the anus for discharge; speech for particular sounds.
They know motion as fivefold; thus these eleven; the mind should be released by intellect.
The ears, sound and thought: these three in the taking in of hearing; so too in touch, in form, and in taste and smell.
So these five triads are qualities for apprehension; by which a threefold state arises in turn.
Sattvic, rajasic and tamasic: these are the three, in which threefold feeling, the means of all, arises.
Joy, love, bliss, happiness, calm thought, arising from no cause or some cause in the mind: the quality of sattva.
Discontent, torment, grief, greed and impatience are the marks of rajas, seen with and without cause.
Lack of discernment, delusion, heedlessness, sleep and drowsiness occur in some way: the various qualities of tamas.
There, what is joined with joy in body or mind, one should observe as the sattvic state.
And what is joined with torment and brings displeasure to oneself, arising, one should think of as rajas.
And what is joined with delusion in body or mind, beyond reasoning, unknowable, one should take as tamas.
That element has hearing as its support; sound rests on hearing; neither is in the knowledge of sound or of another.
So skin, eyes, tongue and nose as fifth: in touch, form, taste, smell; these are thought and the mind.
The simultaneity of their own actions stays in these ten; know thought as eleventh and intellect as twelfth.
When they are not simultaneous there is no tamasic annihilation; when simultaneous, that is worldly dealing.
Even having let go the senses, having seen the tradition heard before, thinking, he does not go on, joined with the three qualities.
The thought overcome by tamas, quick-moving and unsteady, makes a cessation at the right time; they call that tamasic happiness.
Whatever, joined with tradition, is not wholly stilled, there too he takes up tamas, as if manifest falsehood.
Thus this quality, relying on its own action, has been explained; somehow it acts rightly for some, and for some it does not.
So thinkers on the self call the aggregate the field; the state that stands in the mind is called the knower of the field.
That being so, what annihilation, or how eternal, with all beings acting by nature, with reason?
As rivers going to the ocean give up their manifestations and names, and do not keep their own, such is the end of being.
That being so, whence a name after death, to arise again, when the soul is mingled and grasped in the middle?
He who knows this understanding of liberation and seeks the self, unheedful, is not stained by the unwished fruits of action, like a lotus leaf sprinkled with water.

Freed from many firm bonds, from those arising from offspring and from the gods, when he gives up pleasure and pain, then, freed, he reaches the highest goal, markless; with the blessings of scripture, authority and tradition, he sleeps, beyond fear of old age and death.
When merit is spent and sin gone, and cause and fruit destroyed, the unattached see the great, unstained, markless space, resting thus.
As a spider turning stays when its thread is spent, though thrown, so the freed one gives up sorrow, shattering like a clod striking a mountain.
As a deer leaves its old horn, or a snake its skin, and goes without looking back, so the freed one gives up sorrow.
As a bird, leaving a tree falling into water, flies off unattached, so he, leaving pleasure and pain, freed, reaches the highest goal, markless.
This verse too was sung by the king of Mithila, looking at the fire that had lit hell: "Not even a husk of mine is burnt here"; so the king himself is said to have declared.
This immortal state, the king of Videha, instructed here by Panchashikha himself, having seen all and settled his purpose, roamed supremely happy, free of grief.
He who reads this settled determination of liberation is not diminished, ever sees, and feels no calamity, suffers no pain; he is freed, like the Maithila reaching Kapila."
[Bhishma said:] "Self-control alone the elders praise, those with concentration on scripture, for all classes, especially the brahmana.
For one who is not self-controlled action is not rightly accomplished; action, austerity and the Vedas are all founded on self-control.
Self-control increases energy and is called a purifier; the self-controlled man, free of sin and fear, gains the great.
The self-controlled sleeps happily and wakes happily; he moves happily in the world, and his mind is serene.
Energy is held by self-control; the sharp one does not reach it; he sees many enemies in himself, one by one.
As beings always fear flesh-eaters, so they fear the not self-controlled; to restrain them the Self-born made a king.
In all the stages of life self-control alone is excellent; the fruit in dharma in them is said to be greater in the self-controlled.
I shall tell the marks of those of whom self-control is the sum: freedom from meanness, from violent effort, contentment, faith.
Making no enmity, hospitable, equal to blame and praise, of good conduct, with character, serene of self, self-possessed and wise, he gains honour in the world and goes to heaven after death.
Intent on the good of all beings, he does not hate anyone through agreement; like a great lake unshaken, he is content and serene with wisdom.
The self-controlled one, from whom all beings have no fear and through whom none has fear, becomes worthy of salutation by all beings, a knower.
He does not rejoice in great gain nor grieve in calamity; he of measured wisdom is called self-controlled, twice-born.
Endowed with learning by deeds, auspicious, practised by the good, ever joined with self-control, he enjoys great fruit of it.
Freedom from envy, forbearance, calm, contentment, pleasant speech, truth, giving, freedom from toil: this is not the way of the evil-minded.

Having brought desire and anger under control, a celibate, master of his senses, exerting himself in fierce austerity, the brahmana of strict vows, awaiting the time, would roam the worlds like a self-possessed man without harm."
[Bhishma said:] "Those endowed with vows not stated in the Veda, eating and doing their business, those who eat what the Veda prescribes, have broken vows, Yudhishthira."
[Yudhishthira said:] "This which ordinary people call austerity, fasting: is this austerity, great king, or what is austerity?"

[Bhishma said:] "What people think austerity by fasting for months and fortnights is injury to one's own self-governance; the good do not hold it as austerity. Renunciation and humility remain the highest austerity.
One should always be fasting, always a celibate, always a sage, always a brahmana, and always worship the deity.
A householder devoted to dharma, ever with sleep, Bharata, should always be a non-eater of meat, and always mutter the purifying prayer.
He should always eat nectar and never eat poison; always eat the remains of the offering, and always be fond of guests."
[Yudhishthira said:] "How can one always be fasting, how a celibate, how an eater of remains, and how always fond of guests?"
[Bhishma said:] "Between the morning and evening meal, he who eats at no other time is ever fasting.
He who eats after servants and guests have eaten, Yudhishthira, enjoys all the nectar; know this.
The twice-born who never eats while others have not eaten wins heaven by that not-eating.
He who eats what remains after gods, ancestors, servants and guests is called an eater of remains.
For them there are endless worlds in the abode with Brahma; the dwellers of heaven come to them with apsarases.
Those who enjoy with gods and ancestors and delight with sons and grandsons have the highest goal."
[Yudhishthira said:] "I doubt whether the Person is the doer of that or not; I wish to hear this in truth from you, grandsire."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Prahlada and Indra, Yudhishthira.
Unattached, his sins shaken off, born in a good family, much learned, free of stiffness and ego, abiding in goodness, devoted to law,
equal in blame and praise, self-controlled, dwelling in an empty house, knowing the origin and dissolution of the moving and the unmoving,
not angry, not glad, among the unpleasant and the pleasant, with equal vision toward gold or clod,
steady in knowledge of his own highest good, of settled resolve, knowing high and low among beings, omniscient and of equal vision,
Shakra, wishing to know, approached Prahlada sitting alone with senses restrained, and, coming to his wisdom, said:

By whatever qualities a man among men is esteemed in the world, we see all those qualities in you without fail.
mahabharata:12:215.11	Bound by snares, fallen from your place, come under the power of your foes, deprived of fortune, Prahlada, you do not grieve over what is to be grieved.
mahabharata:12:215.12	Is it from gain of wisdom, Daitya, or from steadiness, Prahlada, that you are in your natural state though seeing your own calamity?
Thus urged by him, the steadfast one of settled resolve answered in gentle speech, describing his own wisdom.

He who does not understand the activity and withdrawal of beings would have stiffness from childishness; there is no stiffness for one who sees.
mahabharata:12:215.15	By nature they proceed and by nature they withdraw, all states, as states; there is no human purpose.
mahabharata:12:215.16	In the absence of human purpose there is no one who is the doer by himself; one who does by himself might here have pride.
mahabharata:12:215.17	But he who thinks of himself as the doer of good and bad, his wisdom is faulty, I think, ignorant of its own form.
mahabharata:12:215.18	If the Person were the doer, Shakra, for his own good, his undertakings would surely succeed, and he would never be overcome.
mahabharata:12:215.19	For the turning away of the undesired and the non-turning away of the dear are seen; so where is human purpose in those who strive?
mahabharata:12:215.20	We see the coming of the undesired and the arrival of the desired without effort, by nature, for some.
mahabharata:12:215.21	Some are seen to wear the appearance of the best minds, while seeking gain of wealth from the ugly and the dull.
mahabharata:12:215.22	When all qualities, prompted by nature, enter good and bad, what then is the cause of pride in him?
mahabharata:12:215.23	All that is by nature: so I am firmly resolved; my wisdom rests in the self; I have no other view.
mahabharata:12:215.24	But I think good and bad are joined with fruit as born of action; I shall tell the whole sphere of actions; hear it.
mahabharata:12:215.25	As someone, a crow speaking, may know rice, so all actions are marks of nature alone.
mahabharata:12:215.26	He who knows only the modifications and not supreme nature would have stiffness from childishness; there is no stiffness for one who sees.
mahabharata:12:215.27	For one who understands that all states here arise by nature, what will pride or conceit do?
mahabharata:12:215.28	I know the whole rule of dharma and the impermanence of beings; therefore, Shakra, I do not grieve, for all this has an end.
mahabharata:12:215.29	Free of mine-ness, free of ego, free of effort, with bonds released, at ease, detached, I see the origin and dissolution of beings.
mahabharata:12:215.30	For one of trained wisdom, self-controlled, free of craving and hope, there is no toil, Shakra, to one who sees with the knowledge of the world.
mahabharata:12:215.31	I have no love for nature or its modifications, nor hatred; I do not see any hater who today holds me as his.
mahabharata:12:215.32	I desire nothing, Shakra, upward, downward or sideways; in knowledge, in the knowable and in ignorance there is no ease.
[Shakra said:] "By what is this wisdom gained, and by what is peace attained? Tell me that means, Prahlada, truly, as I ask."
[Prahlada said:] "By honesty, heedfulness, serenity, self-possession and service to the elders, Shakra, a man gains the great.
By nature one gains wisdom, by nature reaches peace; by nature is all that you see."
[Bhishma said:] "Thus addressed by the lord of the Daityas, Shakra was astonished, and, pleased then, king, he honoured that speech.
Then, having honoured the lord of the Daityas, the lord of the three worlds took leave of the king of the asuras and went to his own dwelling."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Vasava and Bali, son of Virochana.
Having conquered all the asuras, Vasava approached the Grandfather, bowed with folded hands and asked about Bali.

Bali, whose wealth never fails him as he gives it: I cannot find that Bali; tell me of Bali, Brahma.
mahabharata:12:216.5	He it was who set, who lit the quarters, who rained rains in due time, tirelessly: I cannot find that Bali; tell me of Bali, Brahma.
mahabharata:12:216.6	He was the wind and Varuna, the sun and the moon, he was the fire that warms beings, and the earth: I cannot find that Bali; tell me of Bali, Brahma.
[Brahma said:] "This is not well that you ask, Maghavan; asked, one should not speak falsely; therefore I shall tell you of Bali.
Among camels, or cows, or asses, or horses, lord of Shachi, he will be the best of creatures in an empty house."
[Shakra said:] "If I meet Bali in an empty house, Brahma, should I kill him or not? Instruct me, Brahma."
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed by the blessed one, Mahendra roamed the earth then, mounting Airavata's shoulder, surrounded with splendour.
Then he saw Bali covered in the form of an ass, as the blessed one had told, dwelling in an empty house.
[Shakra said:] "You have been reborn in an ass's womb, Danava, eating chaff; this womb of yours is low, a drying one; do you not grieve?
Alas, I see an unseen thing: one come under the power of foes, bereft of fortune and friends, fallen from valour and prowess.
You who went, surrounded by kinsmen in thousands of vehicles, scorching all the worlds, disregarding us,
the Daityas stood facing you, in your command; the earth yielded without tilling in your sovereignty; this is your calamity now; do you grieve or not?
When you stood on the eastern shore of the ocean, tasting and sharing wealth among kinsmen, how was your mind then?"
A sacrificer, generous, wise, devoted to brahmanas, true to his pledge, not contemptuous, a giver, master of the Veda and its limbs.
Vasava, having conquered and slain all the asuras and gained Indra's rank in the worlds, then chose as his priest Brihaspati, the eldest son of Angiras, best of brahmanas.
Your own son Yuyutsu, best of kings, great king, shall be king, or any other whom you think fit.
Like moths into a fire the Kukuras and Andhakas fell; no one who was being slain thought of flight.
Then Narada, who stood among the host of gods and knew all the worlds, of great austerity, a great speaker, said in a loud voice:
By a trick you deceived Drona about his son; by a trick alone, king, hell was shown to you then.
